title: Fine-Tuning with Trainer
description: Use the Trainer API to fine-tune without a manual loop, configure hyperparameters with TrainingArguments, attach real evaluation metrics, and manage checkpoints and early stopping.

lessons.title: The Trainer API: Training Without a Manual Loop
lessons.description: Use Trainer to fine-tune a model without writing your own training loop.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what the Trainer class does and what pieces you need to hand it.

sections.title: 🔁 The training loop you already know, packaged
sections.content:
The deep learning course had you write a training loop by hand: forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer step, repeated over epochs. The `Trainer` class packages that exact loop, plus checkpointing, logging, and evaluation, behind a configuration object.

```python
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=TrainingArguments(output_dir="out", num_train_epochs=3),
    train_dataset=tokenized["train"],
    eval_dataset=tokenized["validation"],
)
trainer.train()
```

sections.title: 🧠 It's still the same underlying math
sections.content: Nothing about backpropagation, gradients, or optimizers changes underneath `Trainer` — it's the same process from the deep learning course. What changes is who writes the boilerplate: batching, moving tensors to the right device, mixed precision, and gradient accumulation are all handled for you.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Treating Trainer as a black box you never need to understand.** When training goes wrong (loss not decreasing, exploding loss), the deep learning course's mental model of what a training loop does is exactly what helps you debug it.

**Forgetting `eval_dataset`.** Without it, Trainer trains blind — no signal on whether you're overfitting.

**Not setting `output_dir`.** Trainer needs somewhere to write checkpoints and logs; it's a required argument, not optional metadata.

questions.explanation: Trainer wraps the same training loop concepts from the deep learning course (forward/backward/optimizer step) together with checkpointing, logging, and evaluation, so you configure it rather than write the loop by hand.

lessons.title: TrainingArguments and Hyperparameters
lessons.description: Configure the knobs that control how a fine-tuning run actually behaves.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can name the key TrainingArguments and connect them to hyperparameter concepts from the ML course.

sections.title: 🎛️ The knobs that matter most
sections.content:
`TrainingArguments` configures hyperparameters you already know from the machine learning course — learning rate, batch size, number of epochs — plus fine-tuning-specific ones like warmup steps and weight decay.

```python
args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="out",
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    warmup_steps=500,
)
```

sections.title: 🌡️ Why fine-tuning learning rates are small
sections.content: Fine-tuning starts from pretrained weights that already encode useful structure. A large learning rate (like you might use training from scratch) can wreck that structure in a few steps — fine-tuning learning rates are typically much smaller (2e-5 to 5e-5 is common) than training-from-scratch rates.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Copying a from-scratch learning rate for fine-tuning.** This is a common cause of a fine-tuned model performing worse than the base model — the learning rate was too aggressive and destroyed pretrained knowledge (sometimes called catastrophic forgetting).

**Ignoring `per_device_train_batch_size` vs. total batch size.** With multiple devices or gradient accumulation, the effective batch size is larger than this single number.

**Skipping warmup.** Warmup steps gradually ramp the learning rate up at the start of training, which stabilizes early updates — skipping it can cause early training instability.

questions.question: Why are fine-tuning learning rates typically much smaller than learning rates used to train a model from scratch?
options: Smaller learning rates are always used, regardless of context
Fine-tuning starts from pretrained weights that already encode useful structure, and a large learning rate can destroy that structure quickly (catastrophic forgetting)
Smaller learning rates make training run faster
Learning rate has no relationship to whether you're fine-tuning or training from scratch
questions.explanation: Because pretrained weights already encode useful structure, a large learning rate applied during fine-tuning can overwrite that structure in just a few steps, a failure mode often called catastrophic forgetting.

questions.question: What is the effect of warmup steps at the start of training?
options: They have no effect and are purely decorative
They gradually ramp the learning rate up from a low value at the start of training, which stabilizes early updates
They delete the first few batches of data
They only apply when using a GPU
questions.explanation: Warmup steps start the learning rate low and increase it gradually, which helps avoid unstable, overly large early updates before the model's gradients have settled into a reasonable direction.

questions.question: Why might `per_device_train_batch_size=16` not reflect the true total batch size during training?
options: per_device_train_batch_size always equals the total batch size with no exceptions
With multiple devices or gradient accumulation, the effective total batch size is larger than the per-device number
Batch size settings are ignored by Trainer
Total batch size is unrelated to per-device batch size in any way
questions.explanation: per_device_train_batch_size is exactly what it says — the batch size processed on each device (or per accumulation step). Multiple devices or gradient accumulation multiply that number into a larger effective total batch size.

questions.question: Which hyperparameters from the machine learning course does `TrainingArguments` let you configure?
options: Only the model's architecture, nothing else
Learning rate, batch size, and number of epochs, among others
Only the license of the model
Only the dataset's file format
questions.explanation: TrainingArguments configures hyperparameters familiar from the machine learning course — learning rate, batch size, number of epochs — plus fine-tuning-specific ones like warmup and weight decay.

questions.question: Why are fine-tuning learning rates typically much smaller than learning rates used to train a model from scratch?

Smaller learning rates make training run faster on any hardware
Learning rate has no relationship to whether you're fine-tuning or training from scratch
questions.explanation: Because pretrained weights already encode useful structure, a large learning rate applied during fine-tuning can overwrite that structure in just a few steps — a failure mode called catastrophic forgetting.

questions.question: What typical range does this lesson give for fine-tuning learning rates?
options: 2e-5 to 5e-5
There is no typical range mentioned
questions.explanation: The lesson gives 2e-5 to 5e-5 as a common range for fine-tuning learning rates, much smaller than rates typically used when training a model from scratch.

questions.question: What is the effect of warmup steps at the start of training?
options: They have no effect and are purely decorative
They gradually ramp the learning rate up from a low value at the start of training, which stabilizes early updates
They delete the first few batches of training data
They only apply when using multiple GPUs
questions.explanation: Warmup steps start the learning rate low and increase it gradually, helping avoid unstable, overly large early updates before the model's gradients have settled into a reasonable direction.

questions.question: Why might `per_device_train_batch_size=16` not reflect the true total batch size during training?
options: per_device_train_batch_size always exactly equals the total batch size
With multiple devices or gradient accumulation, the effective total batch size ends up larger than the per-device number
Batch size settings are completely ignored by Trainer
Total batch size has no relationship to per-device batch size
questions.explanation: per_device_train_batch_size is the batch size processed on each device (or per accumulation step); multiple devices or gradient accumulation multiply that into a larger effective total batch size.

lessons.title: Evaluating During Training
lessons.description: Attach metrics to Trainer so you can see real performance numbers, not just loss.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can attach a `compute_metrics` function to Trainer and explain why loss alone isn't enough.

sections.title: 📉 Loss is not the metric you actually care about
sections.content:
Training loss tells you the model is fitting its objective, but a stakeholder wants accuracy, F1, or another metric from the machine learning course's evaluation toolkit — not a raw loss number. `compute_metrics` is a function you supply that turns model predictions into metrics like these.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    preds = logits.argmax(axis=-1)
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, preds),
        "f1": f1_score(labels, preds, average="weighted"),
    }
```

sections.title: 📊 Setting evaluation strategy
sections.content: `TrainingArguments(eval_strategy="epoch")` (or `"steps"`) tells Trainer when to run evaluation during training, so you see metrics evolve over time rather than only at the very end — exactly the kind of overfitting-detection curve discussed in the deep learning course.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Only checking final metrics, never the trend.** A model that overfits shows validation metrics that improve then degrade — you only see this by evaluating periodically, not just once at the end.

**Using accuracy on an imbalanced classification task.** As in the ML course, accuracy can be misleading on skewed classes — F1 or per-class metrics tell a fuller story.

**Forgetting metrics need the raw predictions, not just loss.** `compute_metrics` receives logits and labels — you must convert logits to predicted classes yourself (e.g. with argmax).

questions.question: Why isn't training loss alone a sufficient signal of model quality?
options: Loss is actually the only thing that matters, nothing else is needed
Loss shows how well the model fits its training objective, but stakeholders usually need interpretable metrics like accuracy or F1 that loss alone doesn't directly convey
Loss and accuracy are always identical values
Loss cannot be computed during training, only after
questions.explanation: Training loss reflects optimization progress on the loss function, but real-world usefulness is usually judged with concrete metrics like accuracy or F1 — which is exactly why compute_metrics exists to compute them separately.

questions.question: What does setting `eval_strategy="epoch"` let you observe that a single final evaluation would not?
options: Nothing different — it has no effect
How validation metrics evolve over the course of training, which can reveal overfitting as performance improves then degrades
The exact license of the model being trained
The total training time only
questions.explanation: Evaluating at each epoch produces a trend over time, letting you see if validation performance starts declining while training loss keeps improving — a classic sign of overfitting covered in the deep learning course.

questions.question: Why might accuracy alone be a misleading metric for an imbalanced classification fine-tuning task?
options: Accuracy is always the best metric regardless of class balance
On a skewed dataset, a model can achieve high accuracy just by favoring the majority class, exactly the pitfall covered in the ML course's metrics lesson
Accuracy cannot be computed for text classification tasks
Imbalance has no effect on any evaluation metric
questions.explanation: Just as the machine learning course covered, accuracy can look deceptively high on imbalanced data because predicting the majority class often already achieves a high accuracy score without the model learning anything useful about the minority class.

questions.explanation: Training loss reflects optimization progress, but real-world usefulness is usually judged with concrete metrics like accuracy or F1 — exactly why compute_metrics exists to compute them separately.

questions.explanation: compute_metrics receives logits and labels; you must convert the logits into predicted classes yourself (e.g. with argmax) before computing metrics like accuracy or F1.

options: Nothing different at all — it has no effect
How validation metrics evolve over the course of training, which can reveal overfitting as performance improves then degrades

questions.explanation: Evaluating at each epoch produces a trend over time, letting you see if validation performance starts declining while training loss keeps improving — a classic overfitting sign from the deep learning course.

options: Accuracy is always the best metric regardless of class balance
On a skewed dataset, a model can achieve high accuracy just by favoring the majority class

questions.question: What mistake does this lesson warn against regarding when you check evaluation metrics?
options: Checking metrics too frequently, which the lesson says should never be done
Only checking final metrics and never the trend, which can hide an overfitting pattern that appears mid-training
Checking metrics is entirely optional and can always be skipped
Metrics should only ever be checked before training begins
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that only checking final metrics misses the trend — a model that overfits shows validation metrics improving then degrading, visible only through periodic evaluation.

lessons.title: Checkpoints, Callbacks, and Early Stopping
lessons.description: Save training progress safely and stop automatically when a model stops improving.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what checkpoints protect against and how early stopping prevents wasted training time.

sections.title: 💾 Checkpoints are training insurance
sections.content:
Trainer periodically saves **checkpoints** — snapshots of model weights and optimizer state — so a crash, timeout, or bad run doesn't cost you the entire training run. `save_strategy` and `save_total_limit` in TrainingArguments control how often and how many checkpoints are kept.

```python
args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="out",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    save_total_limit=2,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="f1",
)
```

sections.title: ⏹️ Early stopping saves time and prevents overfitting
sections.content:
An `EarlyStoppingCallback` monitors a chosen metric and stops training if it hasn't improved for a set number of evaluations — directly connected to the deep learning course's discussion of stopping training before a model overfits.

```python
from transformers import EarlyStoppingCallback

trainer = Trainer(
    ..., callbacks=[EarlyStoppingCallback(early_stopping_patience=2)]
)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Not setting `load_best_model_at_end=True`.** Without it, the *last* checkpoint is used even if an earlier one scored better on your chosen metric.

**Choosing the wrong `metric_for_best_model`.** If you care about F1 but track loss, 'best' checkpoint selection optimizes for the wrong thing.

**Setting `save_total_limit` too low with frequent saves.** You can accidentally delete a checkpoint you wanted, if the limit is smaller than expected.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of periodically saving checkpoints during training?
options: Checkpoints have no practical purpose
They protect against losing all training progress if a crash, timeout, or bad run interrupts training
Checkpoints only exist to slow down training
Checkpoints replace the need for a validation set
questions.explanation: Checkpoints are periodic snapshots of model and optimizer state. If training is interrupted, you can resume from the last checkpoint instead of losing all progress and starting over.

questions.question: What does `EarlyStoppingCallback` do?
options: It stops training immediately after the first epoch, always
It monitors a chosen metric and stops training if it hasn't improved for a set number of evaluations, saving time and reducing overfitting risk
It deletes all saved checkpoints
It only works with image models
questions.explanation: Early stopping watches a metric (like validation F1) over successive evaluations, and halts training once it stops improving — directly connected to preventing the overfitting pattern covered in the deep learning course.

questions.question: Why is `load_best_model_at_end=True` important if you care about picking the best checkpoint?
options: It has no effect on which checkpoint is used
Without it, Trainer returns the last checkpoint by default, even if an earlier checkpoint scored better on your chosen metric
It's only relevant for very large models
It automatically deletes all checkpoints except the best one immediately
questions.explanation: Without this flag, Trainer's final model is simply whichever checkpoint came last chronologically — not necessarily the one that scored best on your chosen metric. Setting it to True ensures the best-performing checkpoint is what you end up with.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of periodically saving checkpoints during training?
options: Checkpoints have no practical purpose at all
They protect against losing all training progress if a crash, timeout, or bad run interrupts training
Checkpoints exist only to slow down training intentionally
Checkpoints replace the need for a validation set entirely
questions.explanation: Checkpoints are periodic snapshots of model and optimizer state; if training is interrupted, you can resume from the last checkpoint instead of losing all progress.

questions.question: What does `EarlyStoppingCallback` do?
options: It stops training immediately after the very first epoch, always
It monitors a chosen metric and stops training if it hasn't improved for a set number of evaluations
It permanently deletes all saved checkpoints
It only functions with image-based models
questions.explanation: Early stopping watches a chosen metric (like validation F1) over successive evaluations and halts training once it stops improving, connecting directly to the deep learning course's overfitting discussion.

questions.question: Why is `load_best_model_at_end=True` important if you care about picking the best checkpoint?
options: It has no effect on which checkpoint ends up being used
Without it, Trainer returns the last checkpoint by default, even if an earlier checkpoint scored better on your chosen metric
It's only relevant when training extremely large models
It automatically deletes every checkpoint except the very first one
questions.explanation: Without this flag, Trainer's final model is simply whichever checkpoint came last chronologically, not necessarily the best-performing one — setting it to True ensures the best checkpoint is what you end up with.

questions.question: What risk does choosing the wrong `metric_for_best_model` create?
options: There is no risk; any metric works identically for checkpoint selection
If you care about F1 but track loss instead, 'best' checkpoint selection ends up optimizing for the wrong thing
It only affects how checkpoints are named, not which is selected
This setting has no relationship to checkpoint selection at all
questions.explanation: Since load_best_model_at_end relies on metric_for_best_model to decide which checkpoint is 'best,' tracking the wrong metric means the selected checkpoint may not actually be the one you care most about.

questions.question: What can happen if `save_total_limit` is set too low with frequent saves?
options: Nothing — save_total_limit has no practical effect
You can accidentally delete a checkpoint you wanted to keep, since only a limited number are retained
Training automatically stops the moment the limit is reached
The model's accuracy degrades as a direct result
questions.explanation: With a low save_total_limit and frequent saving, older checkpoints get deleted to stay under the limit, which can accidentally remove a checkpoint you actually wanted to keep.
